text:
LEGO Star Wars | Source: TT Games / Warner
Gaming at LEGO turned 30 last year . The company noted the milestone in its record 2025 results (DKK 83.5B in revenue, up 12%, at a 26% operating margin), where "Gaming at LEGO" covers both digital and physical products: from AAA games on consoles to gaming-IP bricks on the shelf. For most, LEGO is best known as the bricks we've played with since childhood, plus the series of adorable IP-driven video games starting in the early 2000s. Closer observers might also be aware of the LEGO Fortnite integration since 2023. Collectively, LEGO's gaming ecosystem is far more storied and expansive.
LEGO Group financial results 2025 | Source: LEGO
The portfolio includes more than 200 games across three decades . Today we see a console franchise whose latest entry is the best-reviewed LEGO game ever made, a Fortnite mode that has logged over a billion player hours, seven Roblox collaborations pulling roughly 480M monthly plays , a $1B stake in Epic Games , and a year-old London studio in stealth mode. This is the story of LEGO's gaming roots, how it is quietly starting to change, and what comes next.
Lost Pieces
LEGO Creator | Source: LEGO, Superscape
LEGO’s earliest digital titles, LEGO Island and LEGO Creator, were built on the premise that players wanted digital sandboxes. LEGO Universe followed the same philosophy. The $125M building MMO that launched in 2010, pulled in 2.3M registered players, and then closed inside 15 months when too few of them paid to stay. LEGO Worlds in 2017 was similar, an open build-anything game that sold about 185K copies in its first week , then gradually faded.
Console: Licensed to Build
LEGO Harry Potter | Source: TT Games / Warner
For years, LEGO's own digital efforts stayed, as CEO Niels Christiansen put it, "a little bit fragmented" and "relatively small." In both LEGO Universe and LEGO Worlds, it pursued the "obvious" sandbox-building approach but was ultimately overshadowed by Minecraft. And today, the closest thing LEGO has to a hit games machine is one it does not own.
Starting with the iconic LEGO Star Wars: The Video Game in 2005, TT Games the Warner Bros. studio behind two decades of LEGO Star Wars, Batman, Harry Potter, Indiana Jones, and Marvel games, made the games while LEGO licensed out the brand. Warner's then-CEO said in 2014 that LEGO games had moved more than 100M units for over $2B (which is the last time anyone put a public number on it). The exact revenue split has never been disclosed, but a partnership that has run for twenty years clearly suits both sides. LEGO takes a brand royalty on the games, the same way it pays a royalty to Disney or Warner for the right to make Star Wars and Batman sets in the first place.
LEGO Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight | Source: LEGO / TT Games / Warner
This business is still chugging along. LEGO Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight launched last month as the highest-rated LEGO game ever (84 on Metacritic; 1.2M units sold and $83M in revenue in week one). It was also built in roughly 18 months on Unreal Engine 5 instead of the five-year, crunch-heavy grind behind 2022's Skywalker Saga.
Week 1 sales estimates Steam, PlayStation, Xbox sales | Source: Alinea Analytics
It also ships with a brick hook: physical sets unlock in-game cosmetics , LEGO's first brick-to-game tie-in of its kind since Dimensions (more on that later).
LEGO 2k Drive | Source: 2K Publishing
It’s also worth noting that when TT's exclusivity lapsed in 2022, LEGO handed a multi-game license to 2K , broadening its console portfolio into LEGO racing and sports, starting with LEGO 2K Drive in 2023.
Mobile: Where The Money Isn’t
LEGO: Heroes Unboxed | Source: Gameloft
On mobile, the list of sunset LEGO mobile titles is long: LEGO Quest & Collect (a Nexon RPG, delisted after ~1.9M downloads), Legacy: Heroes Unboxed (Gameloft, killed twice, the second time on Netflix in 2025 ), the Tencent sandbox LEGO Cube that stalled in China… and the list goes on.
LEGO companion apps downloads | Source: Sensor Tower
Companion apps like Builder, Insiders, and education apps together pull around 1.9M downloads a month and earn nothing; they exist to support the physical product. The games LEGO licenses out do earn but barely: across its entire free-to-play mobile catalogue since 2018, net revenue totals roughly $18.7M, a rounding error for a company that books DKK 83.5B ($13B) a year.
LEGO licensed games lifetime downloads and revenue | Source: Sensor Tower
Two-thirds of that F2P revenue comes from StoryToys’ LEGO DUPLO Marvel, which targets preschoolers and monetizes through a modest subscription and Marvel content packs. It is the only audience where LEGO has let a paid mobile model run, and even there the estimated net revenue is only around $12M.
LEGO Builder’s Journey | Source: Light Brick Studios
Several of its higher-production titles sit on Apple Arcade , where there is no IAP, no ads, and engagement KPIs are undisclosed. Among them: LEGO Star Wars: Castaways , a social multiplayer game that shipped in 2021 and was quietly sunset by 2023, and LEGO Builder's Journey , a meditative, Monument Valley-style puzzler. Even Hill Climb Adventures , LEGO and Fingersoft's one genuinely free-to-play swing in 2024, netted only about an estimated $365K and shipped with an ad-free Arcade edition alongside it.
LEGO Hill Climb Adventures | Source: Fingersoft
Whether that reflects deliberate policy (protecting a trusted brand from aggressive monetization) or plain economics (preschool parents may be the only audience where the subscription math and the CPIs work), the result is the same. Mobile is a brand channel. The bricks are the business.
Epic Playdates
LEGO Fortnite | Source: Epic
TT Games went four years between mainline console releases, but LEGO gaming was not idle. LEGO Fortnite launched in December 2023 and briefly drew 2.45M concurrent players , a weekend bigger than Fortnite's own Battle Royale. It has stayed busy: a survival mode (Odyssey) and a social mode (Brick Life), a two-part Ninjago expansion across late 2025 and 2026, and a Star Wars Mandalorian crossover in May.
LEGO Fortnite CCU | Source: fortnite.gg
The engagement is real: Odyssey has logged over a billion player hours, even if its concurrent players now sit in the 8,000 to 23,000 range on a typical day, eighth on Fortnite's most-played board (Brick Life barely registers, at around 1,600). Revenue is harder to pin down, because LEGO and Epic don't break it out, and how much of it reaches LEGO is another question. Odyssey and Brick Life are Epic-published modes, so their item-shop spending flows to Epic, and LEGO's 15% share applies only to creator-built LEGO Islands, with the LEGO-branded corners of Fortnite carrying lighter monetization than the rest of the game. For LEGO, revenue was likely secondary, and what matters most is successfully building brand affinity with millions of players, including the younger generation.
CCU during LEGO collabs with various Roblox titles 2025/2026 | Source: CreatorExchange
Roblox is the quieter second front. Over the past year LEGO ran (at least) seven licensed events inside top experiences (Fisch, Driving Empire, Sonic Speed Simulator, and others) reaching about 480M monthly plays, all built by outside studios like Gamefam and Voldex.
Driving Empire x LEGO Batman collaboration | Source: Driving Empire
In addition to simple brand exposure, LEGO appears to be thoughtful about the timing of these Roblox collaborations. For example, Sonic Speed Simulator's concurrent players roughly doubled during a 2025 LEGO event that coincided with a new wave of LEGO Sonic brick sets launching, and the Batman crossover in Driving Empire coincided with the recent console game launch.
Physical Fortnite sets contain DLC codes | Source: LEGO
LEGO is driving brand awareness and engagement on both of the leading platforms for kids games. On Roblox, coordinated collaborations with leading titles can be more surgical short-term marketing activities for new toy or AAA game launches. Fortnite (in which LEGO is significantly invested) is a longer-term strategy — a multi-year destination where kids (and adults) can build brand affinity over time, in both on and offline play (LEGO Fortnite bricks also contain DLC for the game). Both plays are valid, and will likely continue to evolve over time.
Phygital: Chip Of The Ol’ Block
LEGO Hidden Side — a short-lived AR LEGO line | Source: LEGO
The third front is the most LEGO of all: wiring the brick itself to a screen, resulting in several more high-profile hits and misses. LEGO Dimensions (2015) entered the toys-to-life category after Skylanders and Disney Infinity proved the demand, sold about four million copies in four months, then died with the whole category inside two years (Disney took a $147M write-down and shut its studio; Skylanders , once a $3B franchise , was also shelved).
Interactive Mario reacts to different “level elements” | Source: LEGO Youtube
LEGO Super Mario (2020) took a different approach by putting the technology inside the brick itself. Players build physical courses using interactive bricks and a Mario figure that responds to coins, enemies, and other elements. While a companion app exists, the core gameplay takes place away from the screen.
The concept proved successful. The line has remained active for six years, a relatively long run for a LEGO theme, although sales have gradually tapered over time. The electronics are set to retire in 2027 as Mario becomes a standard minifigure. While the interactive Mario line may be nearing its conclusion, the technology behind it remains central to LEGO's future plans.
Star Wars SMART Play | Source: LEGO
This year, LEGO unveiled SMART Play , essentially "version 2" of the above. As Creative Play Lab SVP Tom Donaldson put it , "LEGO Super Mario was tremendously successful for us, but it was also challenging because it wasn't a platform." SMART Play is the platform answer: one patented chip and a Bluetooth protocol meant to run across themes instead of rebuilding the tech for each line. It is eight years and 20 patents in the making, and product chief Julia Goldin has likened it to a games console .
Pokemon SMART Play | Source: LEGO
Unfortunately, initial signals are mixed, citing price (too much) and fun (not enough). The Star Wars launch sets were 20-36% off on Amazon within twelve weeks, unusual for LEGO at that age, with sub-three-star ratings and some weak reviews. Twelve Pokémon SMART Play sets follow in August, and their holiday sales are the real test of whether the platform earns a third wave.
LEGO Digital Play: Beyond the Brick?
For decades, LEGO has smartly relied on licensing, letting others build LEGO-themed video games. LEGO Digital Play may mark the return of first-party games again. Set up in early 2025, it is run by Aaron Loeb (Scopely's chief business officer between 2020 and 2023), with a small, senior team: Bjorn Book-Larsson (ex-Roblox and Epic, where he ran avatar and identity work), Christine Brownell (a sandbox designer whose career runs from WoW to Media Molecule), and Raffaele Fragapane (an ex-Epic MetaHuman lead who rigged characters for The LEGO Movie in 2014).
The funding behind it is real and growing. The "Other LEGO Holding activities" line-item expense more than doubled to DKK 2. 1B ($3 30M) in 2025 , with the holding company naming "developing a digital play organisation" as a driver. LEGO Group's CFO is listed as managing director of the LDP holding entity, and Group CEO Niels Christiansen said LEGO will now make its games in-house and that he would "almost rather overinvest." This signals the end of the pure license-it-out era.
So what is LDP building? Loeb won't say and won't even commit to bricks stating that "it might not even be brick-based." He has framed the goal as a long-term, systemic place for the brand in digital, not another quick release. LEGO is not even completely focused on kids. As early as 2021 LEGO's then-VP of games, Sean McEvoy, said the company bet that LEGO Digital Play could reach "broader and more inclusive audiences ... more adults, a more diverse and inclusive kids audience, and more preschoolers."
The early guess is something mobile- and Roblox-shaped, but whatever route is pursued, LDP has to navigate the brand expectations. LEGO is the name parents already hand to their kids without a second thought, and that needs to be preserved.
Aside from new revenue, a first-party LEGO platform and games would let the company own the player relationship and the first-party data it has always handed to Epic, Roblox, and retailers. Until anything is announced, we can only speculate on the details.
All the Pieces are in Place
The LEGO Movie 2 | Source: Warner Animation
LEGO’s video game strategy is perhaps stronger and more diverse than it’s ever been before. It will continue launching mainline console and PC games, build out its Fortnite experiences, market through third-party experiences on Roblox, and rethink its first-party strategy. LEGO has 30 years of gaming successes and setbacks to draw lessons from, and we’re excited to see what LEGO Digital Play spins up. Whether it can produce a breakout hit remains to be seen, but we expect continued evolution. LEGO's gaming ambitions are entering a new phase. The company has the talent, capital, experience, and brand recognition to pursue them, and the next few years should reveal just how far it intends to go.

Source: gamesindustry.biz

The game, an RPG based on wuxia and Chinese mythology, launched on Steam in Early Access on September 20, 2018, at a point when Steam's Chinese audience had rapidly expanded to more than 30 million users. Niko Partners analyst Daniel Ahmad noted at the time that Steam had originally gained popularity in China thanks to the rise of Dota 2, but the addition of more China-developed and Chinese language games, as well as regional pricing and local payment methods, had helped attract more gamers from the nation.”
Own Your Players, Don’t Rent Them — D2C, Creator Codes & the Shadow Server Economy | Liam Wiltshire, GM of Tebex (GameMakers): “Epic spent five years and over $100M breaking the platforms' 30% tax — then cut V-Bucks by 20% to "pay the bills." When AI makes content infinite and attention stays finite, the only asset that appreciates is the direct relationship with your players — the one distribution channel that gets cheaper the stronger it gets. And a nearly invisible economy of community-run game servers has been proving its dollar value for fifteen years.”
The DEFINITIVE Guide to D2C in 2026: Real Numbers from 8 Studios (two & a half gamers): “Matej Lančarič, Jakub Remiar, and Felix Braberg are joined by Chip Thurston (FastSpring) for a D2C deep-dive built around the Pocket Gamer report aggregating publicly disclosed D2C revenue. Google settlement and its 20% linked-payment fee, where Apple's appeals stand after the Supreme Court declined to hear them, and the single most actionable takeaway: maximize US D2C traffic today, while you can still steer without fees. The window is open right now. It won't stay open forever.”
The Big Xbox Matthew Ball Interview: “T he Console Market Is Not Dying” (The Game Business): “This edition of The Game Business Show is with Xbox Chief Strategy Officer Matthew Ball, recorded on stage at The Game Business Live on Monday, June 8. In this candid conversation with the Xbox leader, Ball shares the thinking and vision behind console exclusives, the frightening DRAM crisis, China, in-game advertising, streaming, working with Asha Sharma and the future of his famous industry reports. ”
Dosa Divas’ Chandana Ekanayake Talks Food, Music, and Indie Development (The AIAS Game Maker’s Notebook): “Alexa Ray Corriea chats with Chandana Ekanayake of Outerloop Games. Together they discuss developing his newest game Dosa Divas, including the origin of the narrative and using food as a storytelling device; weaving together story with combat; the importance of the introductory hour of gameplay; his views on risk and team size; and his thoughts on working in indie development.”
Wh y “D on’t Rock the Boat” Fails Game Dev Teams (Building Better Games): “Many game dev leads survive by following a simple, unwritten rule: don't rock the boat. But staying silent when you see a broken system isn't "playing it smart,” it’s dodging your responsibility. True leadership isn't about having a perfect record or a flawless game plan; it’s about having the courage to stand in the public square, plant a flag, and risk being wrong for the sake of your team. In this episode, Benjamin Carcich breaks down the uncomfortable reality of what it actually means to lead in an agency-based industry like game dev. He exposes the two primary traps leaders fall into when trying to avoid vulnerability - hiding in plain sight or forcing absolute compliance - and shares a personal story of failure that forced him to choose between self-preservation and the work.”

Aside from new revenue, a first-party LEGO platform and games would let the company own the player relationship and the first-party data it has always handed to Epic, Roblox, and retailers. Until anything is announced, we can only speculate on the details.

All the Pieces are in Place

LEGO’s video game strategy is perhaps stronger and more diverse than it’s ever been before. It will continue launching mainline console and PC games, build out its Fortnite experiences, market through third-party experiences on Roblox, and rethink its first-party strategy. LEGO has 30 years of gaming successes and setbacks to draw lessons from, and we’re excited to see what LEGO Digital Play spins up. Whether it can produce a breakout hit remains to be seen, but we expect continued evolution. LEGO's gaming ambitions are entering a new phase. The company has the talent, capital, experience, and brand recognition to pursue them, and the next few years should reveal just how far it intends to go.

95% of Dive clients grow revenue in their first year. Content Worth Consuming

The Devs of Chinese Hit The Scroll of Taiwu on What Western Devs Get Wrong in China — and Why They Rejected Generative AI (gamesindustry.biz): “Long before the global success of Genshin Impact and Black Myth: Wukong, The Scroll of Taiwu from ConchShip Games pointed towards the potentially huge market for Chinese-developed titles. The game, an RPG based on wuxia and Chinese mythology, launched on Steam in Early Access on September 20, 2018, at a point when Steam's Chinese audience had rapidly expanded to more than 30 million users. Niko Partners analyst Daniel Ahmad noted at the time that Steam had originally gained popularity in China thanks to the rise of Dota 2, but the addition of more China-developed and Chinese language games, as well as regional pricing and local payment methods, had helped attract more gamers from the nation.”

Own Your Players, Don’t Rent Them — D2C, Creator Codes & the Shadow Server Economy | Liam Wiltshire, GM of Tebex (GameMakers): “Epic spent five years and over $100M breaking the platforms' 30% tax — then cut V-Bucks by 20% to "pay the bills." If the company that won the fee war still gets squeezed, what does that say about everyone else? The answer isn't about fees. When AI makes content infinite and attention stays finite, the only asset that appreciates is the direct relationship with your players — the one distribution channel that gets cheaper the stronger it gets. And a nearly invisible economy of community-run game servers has been proving its dollar value for fifteen years.”

The DEFINITIVE Guide to D2C in 2026: Real Numbers from 8 Studios (two & a half gamers): “Matej Lančarič, Jakub Remiar, and Felix Braberg are joined by Chip Thurston (FastSpring) for a D2C deep-dive built around the Pocket Gamer report aggregating publicly disclosed D2C revenue. They break down the three cohorts (social casino, mid-core, casual) and what each tells us, the standout data points (Playtika at 39% of revenue, Fishing Clash at 33%, Double Down at 44%), the difference between direct-checkout links and web stores and why you need both, Google's new External Content Links policy, the still-unapproved Epic v. Google settlement and its 20% linked-payment fee, where Apple's appeals stand after the Supreme Court declined to hear them, and the single most actionable takeaway: maximize US D2C traffic today, while you can still steer without fees. The window is open right now. It won't stay open forever.”

The Big Xbox Matthew Ball Interview: “The Console Market Is Not Dying” (The Game Business): “This edition of The Game Business Show is with Xbox Chief Strategy Officer Matthew Ball, recorded on stage at The Game Business Live on Monday, June 8. In this candid conversation with the Xbox leader, Ball shares the thinking and vision behind console exclusives, the frightening DRAM crisis, China, in-game advertising, streaming, working with Asha Sharma and the future of his famous industry reports. ”

Dosa Divas’ Chandana Ekanayake Talks Food, Music, and Indie Development (The AIAS Game Maker’s Notebook): “Alexa Ray Corriea chats with Chandana Ekanayake of Outerloop Games. Together they discuss developing his newest game Dosa Divas, including the origin of the narrative and using food as a storytelling device; weaving together story with combat; the importance of the introductory hour of gameplay; his views on risk and team size; and his thoughts on working in indie development.”

Why “Don’t Rock the Boat” Fails Game Dev Teams (Building Better Games): “Many game dev leads survive by following a simple, unwritten rule: don't rock the boat. But staying silent when you see a broken system isn't "playing it smart,” it’s dodging your responsibility. True leadership isn't about having a perfect record or a flawless game plan; it’s about having the courage to stand in the public square, plant a flag, and risk being wrong for the sake of your team. In this episode, Benjamin Carcich breaks down the uncomfortable reality of what it actually means to lead in an agency-based industry like game dev. He exposes the two primary traps leaders fall into when trying to avoid vulnerability - hiding in plain sight or forcing absolute compliance - and shares a personal story of failure that forced him to choose between self-preservation and the work.”

title: Epic: “We’re going to all need to change the way we build things” – The Game Business Micro
author: Christopher Dring
excerpt: We report on the State of Unreal address, and chat to Shift Up CEO Kim Hyung-tae
text:
Happy Monday! And welcome to The Game Business Micro.
The Micro is our mini-news and analysis episode of The Game Business Show. Whereas our main shows on Tuesday and Thursday are free, the Micro is for paid subscribers only. It comes out once a week, and features a bit of analysis of the big stories from the previous seven days.
This week, I discuss Epic’s State of Unreal address, and share some quotes from a recent interview with Kim Hyung-tae, the CEO of Stellar Blade developer Shift Up.
Enjoy!
Epic issues AAA and Roblox warning as it reveals Unreal Engine 6
In Brief: Epic boss Tim Sweeney called on the video game industry to connect together and change how it makes games to counter a future where “Roblox grows and eats gaming”.
During the firm’s State of Unreal Address, he said: “What you have [with Roblox] is a centralized platform that has a single gatekeeper that commoditises everything and takes more than 70% of the revenue generated by 450 million users. That’s a real challenge.”
He talked about how the next generation of gamers are more socially connected, and that modern AAA games are costing too much to make and not generating enough in return.
“We’re going to all need to change the way we build things,” he told the audience. “We’re going to need to build better games. We’re going to need to build them more efficiently. And we’re going to need to design upfront and build for connected games, where all of our player bases are connected socially and our economies are connected, so that players, instead of seeing these as isolated products, see them as part of a global ecosystem that all game developers participate in together.”
What You Need To Know:
Unreal Engine 6 will allow developers to create games of all sizes and deploy them across Fortnite, traditional game platforms, and their own multi-product ecosystems. It will bring together Epic’s normal Unreal Engine with the Unreal Editor for Fortnite products.
Epic said that Unreal Engine 6 will allow Fortnite skins (plus other assets) to be used in other UE6 games via a system called Smart Assets.
Unreal Engine 6 will integrate Claude, Gemini, and others AI tools as ‘creativity and productivity multipliers’. UE6 will also move the gameplay programming model to Verse.
Unreal Engine 5.8 has added a plugin that will enable developers to connect models like Claude directly into existing Unreal Engine productions.
UE 5.8, which is expected to be the final Unreal Engine 5 update (but that may change), features a string of new additions, including improvements for games on Nintendo Switch 2.
Since Epic launched Unreal Editor for Fortnite, the firm has paid out over $1 billion to creators.
Having already added Star Wars to UEFN (where creators can make their own Star Wars games), The Simpsons is the next IP to be added to the platform.
Meanwhile, the company reminds us that the Epic Games Store now has more than 6000 games from more than 3000 partners. Player spend on third-party PC games on the store is up 57% in 2025, reaching $400 million.
My Take
Tim Sweeney is great at generating a headline. In one relatively short closing remark, he addressed the unsustainability of AAA development, suggested the next-generation will want entirely different games, and declared war on Roblox.
Of course, he was generalizing. The industry has moved on plenty since the 1990s when the audience for video games was largely confined to a handful of demographics. Everyone is a gamer now, and that means there is a variety of different futures for this business. Yes, hundreds of millions do want Roblox-like social experiences. But there are also hundreds of millions who do not. Yes AAA game development is unsustainable, except for the AAA games that aren’t.
Regardless, Sweeney’s speech is, of course, a sales pitch. He pointed to all the problems facing video game companies. And how do we fix these problems? Why, Unreal Engine 6, of course.
